verses.text: As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer's oil, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
A wise man's heart inclines to the right, but the heart of a fool to the left.
Even as the fool walks along the road, his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.
If the ruler's temper flares against you, do not abandon your post, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun— an error that proceeds from the ruler:
Folly is appointed to great heights, but the rich sit in lowly positions.
I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.
He who digs a pit may fall into it, and he who breaches a wall may be bitten by a snake.
The one who quarries stones may be injured by them, and he who splits logs endangers himself.
If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success.
If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer.
The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool consume him.
The beginning of his talk is folly, and the end of his speech is evil madness.
Yet the fool multiplies words. No one knows what is coming, and who can tell him what will come after him?
The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.
Woe to you, O land whose king is a youth, and whose princes feast in the morning.
Blessed are you, O land whose king is a son of nobles, and whose princes feast at the proper time— for strength and not for drunkenness.
Through laziness the roof caves in, and in the hands of the idle, the house leaks.
A feast is prepared for laughter, and wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything.
Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, or curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech.

context.author: “The Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1); in Hebrew Qoheleth, “one who gathers” or “speaks to an assembly.” The book never names Solomon. Jewish and Christian tradition read it as Solomon; many scholars think a later writer took Solomon’s voice, because the Hebrew looks late and the speaker talks of kings before him in Jerusalem (1:16).
context.genre: Wisdom reflection: a searching first-person essay with poems and proverbs
context.audience: Anyone trying to find meaning in work, pleasure, wisdom and wealth, and finally “my son” (12:12)
context.setting: This chapter is a collection of proverbs. “As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor” (v.1). The fool shows everyone he is a fool just by walking down the road (v.3). If a ruler is angry, stay calm at your post (v.4). The world is upside down: folly set on high, “slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot” (vv.6-7). Ordinary work has its risks: he who digs a pit may fall in it, he who splits logs may be hurt, but “if the axe is dull… skill produces success” (vv.8-10). The fool talks on and on (vv.12-14). Woe to a land whose king is a child and whose princes feast in the morning (vv.16-17). “Through laziness the roof caves in” (v.18). And be careful what you say, even in your bedroom, “for a bird of the air may carry your words” (v.20).
context.custom: Perfumers mixed spices into oil, and flies drawn to it could spoil a whole batch (v.1). Snake charmers performed with snakes (v.11). Flat roofs of beams covered with packed earth had to be rolled and repaired after rain, or they leaked and sagged (v.18). In old Israel the right hand was the place of honor and strength (v.2).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 11 says cast your bread on the waters, sow in the morning, and rejoice in your youth.
context.timelineBible: Proverbs, too, warns against a land with child rulers and drunken princes (Proverbs 31:4-5) and against the slacker’s house (Proverbs 24:30-34). Jesus says what is whispered in inner rooms will be proclaimed from the housetops (Luke 12:3).

translation.meaning: Foolishness. A little of it ruins much wisdom.
Wisdom, skill. Sharpening the axe is wisdom at work.
Sloth, idleness. A sagging roof is its result.

gospelParallels.note: What you whispered in inner rooms will be proclaimed on the housetops.
The tongue is a small part, but a fire.
A little leaven works through the whole batch (v.1).

otBackground.note: He who digs a pit will fall into it.
I will make youths their officials.

overview.summary: A little folly spoils much wisdom; the world is often upside down; skill makes work easier, laziness ruins a house, and careless words travel far.
overview.settingLine: Proverbs for the street, the workshop and the court.

history.t: Young kings were ruled by others.

archaeology.t: Iron axe heads from Iron Age Israel show the tools of woodcutters.
Round stone rollers for packing roofs are found in old houses.

overview.discussion: “A bird of the air may carry your words” (v.20). What have I said in private that I would not want carried?
overview.book: The book of Ecclesiastes · 12 chapters. The Teacher searches for lasting gain “under the sun,” finds everything a breath, and ends: fear God and keep His commandments.
overview.author: The Teacher (Qoheleth)

peoplePlaces.d: Shows his folly on the road
